Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nguyen (Redwood CSM), Maya Lopez (Sunrise Platform Eng), Tom Reed (Sunrise Infra Lead), Asha Mehta (Sunrise SRE), Jordan Kim (Sunrise PM)

Summary (auto):
Quick sync on TTFT and streaming variance from last week's pilot run. Samir walked through kernel selection reasoning and new microburst results. Action items: Redwood to run a larger microburst sample, customer to share prod prompts and seq distribution, follow-up on VPC peering timing.

Topics: TTFT trends, streaming handshake, sequence-length tail behavior, kernel hedging, KV cache validation, VPC peering timing, pilot cost/pricing adjustments.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Carter: Hey everybody thanks for joining. we are at 15:00 PT, I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Samir, and priya from our side. Maya, Tom, Asha, Jordan from Sunrise, can you quick confim we can record?
[00:10] Maya Lopez: Yep that's fine, recorded. thanks Alex.
[00:15] Priya Nguyen: Quick agenda, we'll go over the microburst numbers Samir pulled, then chat kernel choices and streaming handshake, then open for infra questions.
[00:20] Tom Reed: sounds good.
[00:22] Samir Patel: ok I'll jump in. So last run we saw TTFT median at ~58ms for the hosted variant and the dedicated pool was around 44ms. However what stuck out were the 95/99 tails on streaming — microbursts where we saw single token pauses up to 420ms. We suspect two main factors: sequence-length-driven kernel swaps and prefix KV-cache misses.
[00:40] Asha Mehta: can you explain kernel swaps a bit, like what's actually causing swap at runtime?
[00:45] Samir Patel: yeah so our runtime picks a kernel based on the observed sequence length and feature flags — for short sequences we use the small-seq fused attention kernel, for long sequences we pick the multi-window tiled kernel. The problem is when a single request straddles the threshold (e.g., 128 to 130 tokens) the runtime may do a different path mid-stream which causes schedule jitter. also quant path vs float path when we hit a new kv-chunk. sometimes the planner reorders and that adds 20-80ms overhead.
[01:15] Maya Lopez: hmm that matches what we saw in our logs. a few requests spike but most are fine. how does prefix caching factor? we have a lot of near-duplicate prompts.
[01:24] Samir Patel: If the KV cache key hashes don't align (we saw some normalization differences in your echoing of prompts), the prefix cache misses and we end up reconstructing kv which adds latency. there's also a small chance the transcriber put kv as "KV cash" in logs (laughs) — but you get the idea.
[01:40] Jordan Kim: is that something on our side or Redwood side? like prompt normalization?
[01:45] Samir Patel: a bit of both. Your client side does some whitespace normalization and we do a trim+tokenization with a slightly different tokenizer setting. We'll provide a short snippet to standardize hashing so cache keys align.
[01:55] Tom Reed: ok. on the peering front, our networking team is worried about the VPC peering window, we need a concrete date.
[02:00] Alex Carter: understood. Priya can own that with you.
[02:04] Priya Nguyen: yes I'll follow up on peering windows after the call.

[02:10] Samir Patel: back to kernels — for this next run we tried hedging: we heuristically start with the low-latency kernel and if sequence length grows beyond threshold we spin up the larger kernel in parallel and we switch when it completes. That reduces median TTFT by 10-12ms in most cases but it increases GPU cycles (cost). the tradeoff is predictable low TTFT vs unit cost.
[02:40] Asha Mehta: cost is a concern for us. our finance model won't allow 30% cost overage in pilot. can hedging be limited to only high-value endpoints?
[02:48] Samir Patel: yes, you can route only high-priority routes to hedging. Redwood can attach tags to routes and apply hedging policies per-route.
[02:55] Maya Lopez: last run we saw a weird artifact when streaming: sometimes first chunk arrived fast but second chunk had a 200ms gap, it looked like handshake renegotiation.
[03:05] Samir Patel: that's likely the streaming handshake when the server decides to rebuffer or switch kernels — there's a small window where the streaming buffer drains and we re-sync, that's our worst-case microburst. we've been experimenting with progressive K/N handshake where we pre-allocate streaming buffer and pin small slices to avoid re-sync. it's promising but adds memory pressure.
[03:30] Tom Reed: memory pressure on dedicated nodes or hosted?
[03:33] Samir Patel: more on dedicated where you want strict isolation. hosted has more overcommit but dedicated is constrained to pool capacity.
[03:38] Alex Carter: quick question for Sunrise — what's your 95th/99th SLO target?
[03:42] Jordan Kim: product wants 95th under 120ms TTFT and 99th under 350ms. ideally. we're flexible if we can get consistency.
[03:50] Alex Carter: ok that's helpful, Samir's hedging plus cache standardization should get us close on 95th, 99th we'll need microburst guardrails.

[03:58] Samir Patel: noted. We ran a focused microburst test last night with 500 samples. Results: median 46ms, 95th 110ms, 99th 370ms with a few spikes at 520ms. The distribution suggests rare infra noise plus the kernel swap boundary.
[04:18] Maya Lopez: so the 520ms ones are the ones we want to understand. are those correlated to seq-length or to specific model versions?
[04:24] Samir Patel: mostly correlated to sequences that started at ~120 tokens then grew. we also saw correlation with certain batch sizes when the serving runtime did background compaction.
[04:36] Asha Mehta: background compaction? like GC?
[04:38] Samir Patel: similar concept, runtime compacts kv shards to reduce memory fragmentation; compaction can preempt and cause a small stall if it wins scheduler time. We can throttle compaction windows or schedule them in low-traffic slots.
[04:50] Tom Reed: can we control compaction from our side?
[04:52] Samir Patel: yes, compaction policy is part of the Dedicated config. Redwood can disable compaction during business hours for your pool and run nightly. that increases memory but reduces microbursts.
[05:00] Jordan Kim: good trade.

[05:05] Samir Patel: one other observation — quantized kernels introduce a bit of variance due to per-layer alignment. switching between 8-bit quant and float paths can add jitter. For the pilot we used q4_k_mixed path which reduces cost but increases jitter. If we lock to q4_k static or float static we get smaller variance but higher cost.
[05:30] Maya Lopez: do you have numbers?
[05:32] Samir Patel: yes quick: q4_mixed median 44ms, 99th 380ms; q4_static median 50ms, 99th 320ms; float static median 65ms, 99th 290ms. So you see cost/variance trade-off.
[05:50] Asha Mehta: float static seems high median but tight tail; might be acceptable for certain routes.

[06:00] Alex Carter: price impact? Priya, do you have a rough delta?
[06:04] Priya Nguyen: rough ballpark — moving from q4_mixed to q4_static increases unit cost ~12%, float static ~28% vs q4_mixed. We'll draft a short table in the follow-up.
[06:16] Maya Lopez: can we do hybrid routing — cheaper for bulk inference and float for priority?
[06:20] Alex Carter: yes that's the recommended: prioritize critical routes to float or q4_static and cheap batch for lower priority. Redwood routing supports that.

[06:30] Tom Reed: another infra question — we've noticed a lot of small connections from our side and NAT ephemeral exhaustion during load tests. is there a connection pooling option?
[06:38] Samir Patel: yes you can use session multiplexing we support persistent sessions with keepalive and http/2 multiplexing, that helps. we'll include a sample client config.

[06:50] Jordan Kim: about the hedging policy, you mentioned per-route tags — how do we identify high-value routes? by user or by intent?
[06:57] Samir Patel: you can tag by route name, or pass a priority header. Many customers map intent (billing, login, core features) to high-priority. It integrates with your existing routing layer or with Redwood's API gateway if you use it.

[07:10] Maya Lopez: ok would be helpful to have a decision matrix: cost vs latency vs reliability for the different kernel+quant combos.
[07:16] Alex Carter: we'll send that. Samir, can you also include the script you used to generate the microburst sample?
[07:20] Samir Patel: yes I'll put the script in the results folder, it's a python harness that shards requests across clients to simulate microburst. note it's sensitive to client sub-timing so we'll include run instructions.

[07:30] Asha Mehta: and about security: we've got a short checklist — SAML SSO, KMS integration, audit logs, and data residency. we got your SOC2 doc but will need HSM/KMS details for private deployment.
[07:42] Priya Nguyen: we've got HSM/KMS integration patterns and we can redact specifics in the doc. I'll add that to the share.

[07:48] Tom Reed: one last thing — bench vs prod environment mismatch. our prod uses longer seq lengths; test bench used truncated prompts. we'll share real distributions.
[07:58] Maya Lopez: yes we'll upload the tokenized distribution.

[08:02] Alex Carter: great. quick recap: Redwood runs larger 2k microburst, share script and results CSV; customer shares prompt set and seq-length distribution; Samir and Asha schedule kernel-priority deep-dive; Priya will follow up on VPC peering and security docs; Alex will send pricing table and pilot scope.
[08:22] Jordan Kim: thanks all, that matches our expectations.
[08:25] Alex Carter: ok we'll get those items out this week. thanks everyone.
